Few creatures do so much essential work with so little notice as bees. When a field of sunflowers glows in the summer sun, it is natural (12)______. Yet the real work happens quietly among the blossoms. A single bee visiting hundreds of flowers a day carries pollen from plant to plant, (13)______ over three-quarters of the world's food crops and flowering plants could not reproduce. It is easy to overlook such a service, because nobody sends a bill for it. (14)______.

Sadly, bees are in decline. Experts blame the destruction of natural habitats and the heavy use of pesticides, with climate change likely to make matters worse. In some regions, farmers have already begun to pollinate crops by hand, a slow and costly task (15)______ for free. (16)______. It lies in leaving corners of gardens wild, planting flowers instead of lawns and thinking twice before spraying chemicals.

In short, bees are not a luxury of the countryside; they are part of the machinery that feeds us. That is why protecting them deserves serious attention, since a world without pollinators would be a poorer and hungrier place for everyone.

Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.
Venice is one of the most beautiful cities on Earth, and that is exactly the problem. Only about 50,000 people live in its historic centre, a

community that is outnumbered by visitors many times over. Most of the crowds are day-trippers, who arrive in the morning, photograph the canals and leave by evening, and many step off cruise ships by the thousand. Experts use the term overtourism when the effects of visitors on local life, and on the visit itself, grow so strong that both suffer.

The pressure is felt in almost every corner of daily life. Narrow alleys and water buses are often so crowded that residents struggle to reach work or school on time. Shops that once served neighbours have turned into souvenir stalls, and rising prices and the spread of holiday rentals have pushed many families to the mainland. As the population shrinks, local services such as schools and clinics become harder to maintain. Even the tourists suffer, queuing for hours in the heat to see sights that should bring peace rather than stress.
Authorities have therefore begun to experiment.
In spring 2024, Venice launched a pilot scheme that charges day-trippers five euros to enter the old city on selected peak days, with fines for those who do not pay.
Machu Picchu in Peru takes another approach: no more than 500 people, including support staff, may start the Inca Trail each day.
The Venetian scheme also helps officials, who could only estimate visitor numbers for years, to collect more accurate figures.
Residents and overnight guests are exempt, so the charge falls mainly on those who come for just a few hours.
Not everyone is convinced. Many residents argue that

are being treated like exhibits in a museum, and that a five-euro fee does little to bring families back to the city. Instead, they call for more affordable housing and tighter rules on short-term rentals. Supporters reply that the scheme is only an experiment whose results will guide future decisions. Whatever the outcome, the Venetian debate raises a question that many popular destinations will soon have to answer: how to welcome visitors without losing the very community that makes a place worth visiting.
(Adapted from BBC Travel and Associated Press)

Ask any teenager about mornings and the reply is likely to be a groan. For years, adults put this down to laziness, assuming that young people simply stay up too late and refuse to go to bed on time. Yet sleep scientists now argue that the real explanation lies deeper, in changes that begin in the body at puberty. Understanding these changes, they say, could transform the way schools plan the day.

During adolescence, the body begins to release melatonin, the hormone that signals bedtime, roughly two hours later than it does in childhood. Researchers also report that teenagers' sleep needs are close to
of primary-school pupils, at around nine hours a night.
Because of this shift, a teenager who cannot fall asleep before eleven is responding to biology rather than choosing to stay up.
An alarm set for six o'clock therefore asks young people to be alert at the hour their bodies still consider night.

sleep loss go well beyond yawning in class. Surveys in the United States suggest that most high-school students sleep less than the recommended amount, and tired teenagers are more prone to low mood, poor concentration and car accidents. Schools that have moved their first lesson to 8:30 a.m. or later report better attendance, fewer dropouts and fewer symptoms of depression among students. One medical association has therefore urged high schools not to start any earlier than 8:30.
Even so, the picture is not entirely straightforward. Whether later starts actually raise exam results is still

, and schools face real obstacles, since changing the timetable affects bus routes, sports practice and parents' working hours. Critics also point out that sleep depends on more than school bells: screens, homework and social media all take their toll. The research points not to a miracle cure but to a sensible adjustment, one that makes it easier, though not automatic, for teenagers to get the rest they need.
(Adapted from Los Angeles Times and Psychiatric News)
introducing a new explanation for a familiar problem
blaming teenagers for their unhealthy habits
praising schools that start the day early
